Note, 9 December. Written by Sangeeta, senior teacher, residential school.

Mohan, twenty-five, took over as boys' hostel warden this term. We have been friends since training college. At home he makes paper boats for his nieces and lets them win at ludo. Tonight I saw him make three Class 6 boys stand outside the dormitory in the cold for talking after lights-out. When one, Gopika's younger brother, started to cry, Mohan said, "Crying won't help you." That is not the Mohan I know.

I also know the job: sixty boys, no deputy, a principal who blames the warden for every complaint.

What I did next: I brought the boys inside, then waited until he was calmer. I said, "This isn't how you are at home. I think the job is pushing you somewhere you wouldn't go." He was silent, then asked if I'd help him draft fair rules and raise the need for a deputy with the principal.

qa.q: How many boys does Mohan look after as warden?
qa.a: He looks after sixty boys.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when she saw Mohan with the boys outside the dormitory?
qa.a: Sangeeta was troubled and surprised, since the harsh warden in front of Sangeeta was not the gentle friend who plays ludo with his nieces.

qa.q: Which part of Sangeeta's approach helped Mohan listen?
qa.a: Waiting until he was calmer and linking his behaviour to the pressures of the job, rather than attacking him, let him admit it and ask for help.

qa.q: What was that cold night like for the three Class 6 boys?
qa.a: They were left outside in the cold and told crying would not help, which likely made them feel scared and unprotected by the person meant to care for them.

grounding: A teacher sees a friend become harsh in his warden role, notes it is not how he is at home, and raises it gently while recognising the job's pressures.

Friday night

Saw Deven at work today for the first time. He's a ticket checker on the metro now. A college boy didn't have a valid card, and Deven held him by the elbow in front of the whole platform and said, "People like you think rules are for others." The boy was shaking. Deven's voice was one I'd never heard.

This is the Deven who used to cry at the end of films. Who carries his grandmother's shopping bags without being asked.

My first thought was to message Jasleen, his sister, and say, "Your brother has become a bully." I didn't. I thought about his job: the fines targets, the cameras everywhere, the supervisors listening on radios.

Tonight I called him. I said, "Deven, today on the platform that wasn't you. At home you'd never talk like that. I think the uniform's doing something." Long pause. Then: "I didn't even notice."

- Alka

qa.a: He is a ticket checker on the metro.

qa.a: Alka felt unsure it was fair to blame Deven without thinking about the fines targets, cameras and supervisors that shape his job, so Alka chose to speak to him directly.

qa.a: Alka named the behaviour plainly, reminded him of how he is at home, and linked it to the role, so he could hear it without feeling attacked.
